newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs time-table to push reforms - WEF.
newsitem.headline: India needs time-table to push reforms - WEF.

text.p: Foreign investors would need key signals and a timetable to indicate India's commitment to economic reforms, Claude Smadja, managing director of the Swiss-based World Economic Forum said on Tuesday.

"Investors really need to know what is really the agenda in terms of major steps and deadlines so that they can take a reasonable calculated risk," Smadja told reporters at the end of a two-day economic conference organised by his institution.

Smadja said India needed to approve and bring to fruition some core sector projects like power plants. "For the process of reforms to succeed, you need the notion of critical speed and critical mass," he said.
"Look at what kind of signal you will have if seven fast track projects get through," he added.

He was referring to seven projects for which India's federal government has promised a financial guarantee, ensuring payment to foreign electricity generation companies for power they would sell to financially-weak distribution firms.
Only three have been approved so far. Critics say red tape in approvals has slowed India's economic reform programme started in 1991, which invites foreign investors in a big way.
Fast approvals to power projects or the opening of the state-controlled insurance sector could send the right signals to foreign investors, Smadja said.
"A six to seven percent rate of growth for an emerging economy is not enough and I know that India can do much better than this," Smadja said.

India's gross domestic product (GDP) rose 6.3 percent in 1995/96 (April-March), and is expected to grow by 6.6 percent in 1996/97. New Delhi is aiming for a 7-8 percent annual growth in the medium term.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram had reassured foreign investors on the continuation of economic reforms during the conference, but some foreign delegates raised questions on the pace of reforms.
"The question of translating political aspiration into action has been much more acute this year than previously," Smadja said.
